To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) seedling emergence in three forest herbs is delayed and reduced in the field relative to controlled conditions; and (2) interspecific differences in dormancy levels are responsible for differences in seed-bank longevity.

the timing of seedling emergence of perennial forest herbs is affected by the timing of dispersal and dormancy levels of seeds, but the persistence of the seedbank is also affected by the timing and duration of stratification.
the three species differed in seed bank longevity and germination requirements, which could affect their population dynamics and persistence.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding variation in seed dormancy, germination and seedling emergence of co-occurring wild-harvest medicinal forest herbs.
seed dormancy and germinability in the context of seedling emergence and recruitment in the forest understory, and the implications for conservation and management of these species.
the germination of seeds with MPD and the role of dormancy in the timing of seedling emergence of perennial forest herbs in the wild.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the three species studied have a dormancy that allows them to survive unfavorable periods for seed germination and emergence.

the species in this study have dormancy requirements that are similar in that all require stratification for germination, but that there is a large difference in the amount of stratification that is required.

the species studied have a summer →autumn →winter requirement for seed germination and emergence in spring, but that there are differences in the dormancy levels and the stratification requirement of their seeds.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the species studied here are all adapted to a similar environment but have different strategies to ensure germination and establishment in a variable environment.
species with MPD can have different dormancy levels, and that dormancy levels can be influenced by seed dispersal timing.
the species differ in their ability to form a seed bank and that the species differ also in their dormancy levels and in the timing of their germination.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the timing and duration of dormancy break and germination can vary substantially between co-occurring plant species.
seedling recruitment is not a simple function of seed dispersal timing, and species with MPD can exhibit a range of germination strategies that may influence population dynamics and persistence.
